chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a set of games: tricks, pyramids, grids, products and puzzles. Each game is played with numbers first, the pattern is guessed, and then a letter-number explains why the pattern must hold. Students end each idea by inventing a trick or puzzle of their own.

points.title: Play first, then explain
points.text: Every trick is tried with two or three starting numbers before any letter appears, so the letter explains a pattern the student has already seen.

points.title: Tools only where handling is the idea
points.text: Nine tools, each used once: building a trick, decoding a date trick, a pyramid builder, a shape grid, a calendar frame, a digit arranger, a digit lab for 9, 11, 37 and 1001, a rounds machine, and a swap counter. The remaining tricks and puzzles are taught without a tool because the algebra itself is the move.

points.title: Check by substituting
points.text: Every answer found with a letter-number is put back into the story or the grid to check it.

points.title: Invent your own
points.text: Math Talk prompts ask for new tricks, new calendar shapes and new puzzles, built from the same algebra.

concepts.concept_name: Why the trick always ends on 2

content.text:
6.2 Thinking about 'Think of a Number' Tricks
In Grade 7, we learned about 'Think of a Number' tricks, like this one.
1. Think of a number. 2. Double it. 3. Add four. 4. Divide by two. 5. Subtract the original number you thought of.
I predict you get 2. Am I right? Try it out with different starting numbers. Do you always end up with the same value, 2? Why?
We saw that we can understand such tricks through algebra.
1. Think of a number: x. 2. Double it: 2x. 3. Add four: 2x + 4. 4. Divide by 2: x + 2. 5. Subtract the original number you thought of: x + 2 − x = 2.
Therefore, no matter what the starting number is, the end result will always be 2!

content.text:
Worked example: Try the trick (double, add four, divide by two, subtract the start) with 5 and with 11, then explain with a letter-number why it always ends on 2.
1. Start with 5: 5 × 2 = 10, then 10 + 4 = 14, then 14 ÷ 2 = 7, then 7 − 5 = 2.
2. Start with 11: 11 × 2 = 22, then 22 + 4 = 26, then 26 ÷ 2 = 13, then 13 − 11 = 2.
3. Start with x: double it to get 2x, add four to get 2x + 4, divide by 2 to get x + 2.
4. Subtract the start: x + 2 − x leaves 2, whatever x is.
Answer: It always ends on 2, because the starting number cancels out

content.text:
Let us now look at a different trick of this type.
Shubham: Think of a date. Multiply the month by 5. Add 6. Multiply by 4. Add 9. Multiply by 5. Add the day. Tell me your answer.
Mukta thinks of 26 January and reports 291. Shubham says: You thought of our Republic Day.
How did Shubham figure out the date chosen by Mukta?
Let the month be M and the day be D. Multiply M by 5: 5M. Add 6: 5M + 6. Multiply by 4: 20M + 24. Add 9: 20M + 33. Multiply by 5: 100M + 165. Add the day: 100M + 165 + D.
Mukta's answer was 291. 291 = 100M + 165 + D. 291 − 165 = 100M + D. 126 = 100M + D.
Since D is a day within a month, it is atmost 31 and requires only 2 digits. So the last 2 digits are D and what comes before that is M. In this case, M is 1 and D is 26, i.e., the 26th of January.

content.text:
What about filling in the numbers in this pyramid? Where do we start? Top 60; middle row two blanks; bottom row 12, a blank, 8.
Let us fill the empty boxes with letter-numbers. From the rules for filling up pyramids, we get the following equations. a + b = 60. 12 + c = a. c + 8 = b.
From this, we see that, (12 + c) + (c + 8) = a + b = 60. Hence, 20 + 2c = 60. 2c = 60 − 20 = 40. c = 20.
Once we know c, we can find a and b, and complete the pyramid.

content.text:
Worked example: Fill the four row pyramid with top 50, second row a blank and 22, and bottom row 4, a blank, 6, a blank.
1. Call the bottom blanks p and q: the bottom row is 4, p, 6, q.
2. Third row: 4 + p, p + 6, 6 + q. The 22 is (p + 6) + (6 + q), so p + q + 12 = 22 and p + q = 10.
3. The top is (4 + p) + 2(p + 6) + (6 + q), which is 3p + q + 22, so 3p + q + 22 = 50 and 3p + q = 28.
4. Take p + q = 10 away from 3p + q = 28: that leaves 2p = 18, so p is 9 and q is 1.
5. Third row 13, 15, 7; second row 28, 22; check 28 + 22 = 50.
Answer: Bottom row 4, 9, 6, 1; third row 13, 15, 7; second row 28, 22

3. The top is 3 + 5 = 8.
4. The sequence goes 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so every number in the grid is in it.
Answer: The grid holds 1, 2, 3, 3, 5 and 8; the top is 8; all are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers

content.text:
Figure it Out (number pyramids, question 5): What can you say about the numbers in the pyramid and the number at the top in the following cases? (i) The first four Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers are written in the bottom row of a four row pyramid. (ii) The first 29 Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers are written in the bottom row of a 29 row pyramid.
1. (i) Bottom row 1, 2, 3, 5. Next row 3, 5, 8. Next row 8, 13. Top 8 + 13 = 21.
2. All of them are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, and the top 21 is the 7th number of 1, 2, 3, 5, ...
3. Two neighbours in the sequence add to the number two places further on, so every row is again a run of Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, moved two places along.
4. (ii) Each row moves two places along, so after 28 steps up the single top box is the 57th number of the sequence.
Answer: (i) All are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers and the top is 21 (ii) All are Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers and the top is the 57th number of the sequence

content.text:
Figure it Out (number pyramids, question 6): If the bottom row of an n row pyramid contains the first n Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, what can we say about the numbers in the pyramid? What can we say about the number at the top?
1. Two neighbours of the sequence add to the number two places further on.
2. So each row is a run of Virahanka-Fibonacci numbers, starting two places further along than the row below.
3. The bottom row starts at the 1st number, so the top row, n − 1 steps up, is the number at place 1 + 2(n − 1), which is the (2n − 1)th number.
4. Check: n = 3 gives the 5th number, 8; n = 4 gives the 7th number, 21.
Answer: Every number in the pyramid is a Virahanka-Fibonacci number, and the top is the (2n − 1)th number of the sequence

6.4 Fun with Grids
Calendar Magic
A page from a calendar is given below. Your friend picks a 2 × 2 grid from this calendar, adds the 4 numbers in this grid and tells you the sum.
August 2025 block 6, 7, 13, 14: 6 + 7 + 13 + 14 = 40.
Can we find the 4 numbers in the grid from just knowing this sum?
Let us use algebra. Consider a 2 × 2 grid. Let a represent the top left number. What are the other numbers in terms of a? a, a + 1, a + 7, a + 8.
Adding all four numbers, the sum is a + (a + 1) + (a + 7) + (a + 8) = 4a + 16.
Suppose you are told that the sum is 36. Can you find the 4 numbers in the grid?
4a + 16 = 36. 4a = 20 (subtracting 16 from both sides). a = 5 (dividing both sides by 4).
Now that we have found a, we know that the other three numbers are a + 1, a + 7 and a + 8. Therefore, the grid must be the following: 5, 6, 12, 13.

Worked example: A friend picks three dates one below the other on a calendar page and says their sum is 51. Find the dates.
1. Call the top date a. The dates below it are a + 7 and a + 14.
2. The sum is a + (a + 7) + (a + 14), which is 3a + 21.
3. So 3a + 21 = 51, which gives 3a = 30 and a is 10.
4. The dates are 10, 17 and 24. Check: 10 + 17 + 24 = 51.
Answer: 10, 17 and 24

Worked example: In a grid, three squares make 27 and two circles with a square make 19. Find the square and the circle.
1. Three equal squares make 27, so one square is 27 ÷ 3 = 9.
2. Two circles and a square make 19, so two circles make 19 − 9 = 10.
3. One circle is 10 ÷ 2 = 5.
4. Check: 9 + 9 + 9 = 27 and 5 + 5 + 9 = 19.
Answer: Square 9, circle 5

Fun with Grids: fill the algebra grids: In the following grids, find the values of the shapes and fill in the empty squares. Grid 1: square, square, circle make 27; circle, circle, square make 21; circle, square, circle make a blank. Grid 2: circle, diamond, diamond make 18; diamond, circle, circle make 15; diamond, circle, circle make a blank; the last row is blank under every column.
1. Grid 1: two squares and a circle make 27, two circles and a square make 21.
2. Adding both rows, three squares and three circles make 48, so a square and a circle make 16.
3. Take that from the first row: one square is 27 − 16 = 11, so a circle is 5. The last row is 5 + 11 + 5 = 21.
4. Grid 2: a circle and two diamonds make 18, two circles and a diamond make 15, so a circle and a diamond make 33 ÷ 3 = 11.
5. One diamond is 18 − 11 = 7 and a circle is 4. The third row is 7 + 4 + 4 = 15.
6. Read the last row as column sums: 4 + 7 + 7 = 18, 7 + 4 + 4 = 15, 7 + 4 + 4 = 15, and the corner is 18 + 15 + 15 = 48.
Answer: Grid 1: square 11, circle 5, last row 21. Grid 2: circle 4, diamond 7, third row 15, column sums 18, 15, 15 and 48 in the corner

6. Read the last row as column sums: 4 + 7 + 7 = 18, 7 + 4 + 4 = 15, 7 + 4 + 4 = 15, and the corner is 18 + 15 + 15 = 48.
